tip: 'A casa' with no article means 'home', not 'to a house'. Bare 'casa' = your own home: 'vuelvo a casa' = I head home.
'Termino trabajando' exists but means 'I end up working'. To finish doing something, Spanish needs 'de' + infinitive: 'termino de trabajar' = I finish working.
'Cada dos días' is literally 'each two days' – that's how Spanish says 'every other day'. No word for 'other' needed: you count the interval instead.
'Acordarse de' = to remember. Always reflexive + 'de': 'me acuerdo de ese día'. Dropping 'de' is a common mistake.
'El mapa' is masculine. Not all -a nouns are feminine – 'mapa' is an exception to memorize.
'Interesar': 'me interesan' (plural) – agrees with 'las ofertas'.
Vacation is normally plural in Spanish: 'las vacaciones'. Even one trip takes plural articles and verbs: 'mis vacaciones fueron cortas'.
'El problema' is masculine. Many -ma words from Greek are masculine: 'problema', 'tema', 'sistema', 'programa', 'clima', 'idioma'.
Taking time is 'tardar en': 'tardó tres horas en llegar' = lit. delayed three hours in arriving. English 'to arrive' tempts you toward 'a' – it's always 'en'.
No verb 'to miss' needed: 'perdí el desayuno' – 'perder' means lose AND miss. You 'lose' buses, flights and breakfasts in Spanish.
'Despedir' = to fire someone; add 'se' and it means to say goodbye. 'Se despidió de todos' = he said goodbye to everyone – and that 'de' is mandatory.
'Por' = for the sake of / in honor of: 'brindamos por tu éxito'.
'La moto' – feminine because it's short for 'la motocicleta'. Keeps gender of the full word.
'Tu idea' is the subject and the opinion-holder is just an object: 'me'. Where English reaches for 'I think it's good', Spanish prefers 'me parece bien' – it seems-good to me.
'Del' is the mandatory contraction of 'de + el': never write 'de el'. 'De la' stays separate (no contraction for feminine).
'Usually' isn't an adverb here – it's the verb 'suele'. Spanish conjugates 'soler' + infinitive for habits: 'suele llover' = it tends-to rain.
'Tomar algo' isn't 'take something' – it's the standard invite for going out for a drink. 'Tomar' covers eating and drinking: 'tomar un café', 'una caña'.
Never say 'me gusta tu amigo' unless you fancy him – 'gustar' with people can sound romantic. For plain liking, use 'me cae bien': he 'falls well' on you.
English fakes a past tense for unreal ifs ('if it weren't'); Spanish has a dedicated form. 'Si no llovía' is wrong – an unreal 'si' needs 'lloviera', paired with 'iríamos'.
Spanish doesn't say he IS embarrassed – public speaking gives him shame: 'le da vergüenza'. Emotions here are things that hit you, not things you are.
'Por' + infinitive = still to be done: 'queda mucho por hacer' = there's a lot left to do.
'Por' = via / by means of: 'lo dije por teléfono'. 'Por' for the method of communication.
In 'la vi ayer', 'her' shrinks to 'la' and sits before the verb – object pronouns latch on in front.
Dishes 'carry' their ingredients: 'lleva tomate' = it has tomato in it. Ask '¿qué lleva?' in any restaurant to hear what's inside a dish.
'Sepa', not 'sabe': after 'no hay nadie que...', that person doesn't exist, so Spanish switches to subjunctive. Nonexistent people don't get real-world verb forms.
'Por' for movement through a place: 'caminamos por' = we walked through/around.
'La radio' – feminine in Spain. Can be 'el radio' in some Latin American countries.
'En casa de' = at someone's house (no article needed).
Spanish apologizes by asking: 'pidió disculpas' = requested pardons. You ask for forgiveness rather than offer an apology.
'Al final' shows the mandatory contraction 'a' + 'el' → 'al'. Only with masculine singular 'el'.
